question: What is the V-shaped groove on the tongue that separates the front two-thirds from the back one-third?
explanation: You've got this! The sulcus terminalis is just a clear V-shaped boundary sitting on top of the tongue, neatly dividing the front part from the back root.

question: Why is the small pit known as the foramen caecum so special in early human development?

options.A: It houses the primary taste buds responsible for detecting bitter flavors
options.B: It marks the starting point of thyroid gland development during embryonic life
options.C: It serves as the attachment point for the lingual frenulum
options.D: It provides the main blood supply to the root of the tongue

explanation: Think of the foramen caecum as a tiny starting point where your thyroid gland began its journey before moving down into your neck during pregnancy!

question: What is the main job of the intrinsic muscles found completely inside the tongue?

options.A: Supplying blood to the taste buds
options.B: Protruding the tongue out of the mouth
options.C: Changing the overall shape of the tongue
options.D: Anchoring the tongue to the mandible

explanation: Because intrinsic muscles live entirely inside the tongue, they work like a flexible cushion to change its shape when you talk or swallow.

question: A stroke patient is trying to stick out their tongue, but it keeps pulling to one side. Which muscle is likely affected?
explanation: The genioglossus is our main tongue-poking muscle! When one side gets weak after a stroke, the tongue deviates toward the weaker side.

question: Which type of tongue bumps (papillae) do NOT have any taste buds?
explanation: Filiform papillae are the rough little bumps that give your tongue friction to help grip food—they aren't involved in tasting.

question: How are the large circumvallate papillae arranged on the human tongue?

options.A: Evenly scattered across the entire ventral surface
options.B: A V-shaped row just anterior to the sulcus terminalis
options.C: Parallel folds exclusively along the posterior edges
options.D: A tight cluster strictly at the very tip of the tongue

explanation: Great job! These big vallate papillae form a neat V-shape right in front of the sulcus terminalis near the back of the tongue.

question: Which cranial nerve gives movement (motor control) to almost all the muscles of the tongue?
explanation: Think 'Hypo-glossal' for tongue movement! It's the big boss nerve controlling almost all tongue muscles.

question: If a patient loses their sense of taste on the front two-thirds of their tongue after ear surgery, which nerve was likely nudged?
explanation: The chorda tympani branch of the facial nerve carries taste messages from the front of the tongue and happens to run right through the middle ear.

question: What is the main artery that brings oxygen-rich blood to the tongue?
explanation: Easy to remember—'lingual' means tongue, so the lingual artery is the main blood supplier for tongue tissues!

question: Where does fluid from the very tip of the tongue first drain into the lymphatic system?
explanation: The submental nodes sit right under your chin, making them the first stop for lymphatic drainage from the very tip of the tongue.

question: What is the tongue's main job right at the start of swallowing food?

options.A: Producing digestive enzymes to break down starches
options.B: Sealing off the nasopharynx to prevent nasal regurgitation
options.C: Pushing the food bolus backward against the hard palate
options.D: Opening the upper esophageal sphincter mechanically

explanation: When you swallow, your tongue acts like a natural spatula, pressing food up and back toward your throat.

question: How does the tongue help us speak clearly and pronounce words?

options.A: By controlling the rate of air expelled from the lungs
options.B: By opening and closing the lips to form consonants
options.C: By generating vocal cord vibrations in the pharynx
options.D: By altering its shape and position to interrupt and shape oral airflow

explanation: Our tongue is amazingly nimble—it taps against our teeth and palate to turn breath into clear speech and sounds!
